# LEAD TIME AS A DESIGN PROBLEM
## Reducing quoted delivery from 14 weeks to [6–7] without touching a single certified inspection
**Executive Committee decision document | v1.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *structure*, the governing rule (§3), the decision rights (Appendix A), and the funding of Gate 1. Every quantity in this document is calibrated at Gate 1 and returned to this Committee before any external lead-time commitment is made.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**We are not slow at building; we are slow at waiting.** In an order-to-delivery chain of this type, the fraction of elapsed time in which material is actually being transformed or verified is typically [10–20]%*[target]*; the rest is queue, batch wait, decision wait, material wait, inspection-availability wait, rework loops, documentation assembly and protective buffer. The last compression attempt failed — and produced two years of warranty pain — because it took time out of the [10–20]% that creates and proves the product instead of the [80–90]% that does neither. That mistake is now the constraint on this project: nothing will be believed inside the company until the plan makes it structurally impossible to repeat. So the plan is governed by one rule: **time may be removed only where no material is being transformed and no verification is being performed** (§3, the *Non-Transformation Rule*). Within that rule there are five legitimate lever classes — queue removal, capacity addition, prevention (first-time yield), scope segmentation, and verification *latency* reduction with verification *content* untouched — and one prohibited class: reducing what we inspect. We then stop selling one lead time to everyone: orders are sorted into **three fulfilment lanes** against a deliberately placed customisation decoupling point (§5), so that the [60–70]%*[target]* of demand that is genuinely configurable-from-platform can be quoted at [6] weeks while genuinely engineered orders are quoted honestly from a capacity-slot calendar instead of being hidden inside a padded average. Quality gates are not weakened; they are **accelerated and made non-negotiable in the same instrument**, protected by an automatic trip-wire that freezes all lead-time reduction if first-time yield, escaping defects or audit findings move the wrong way (§7.4) — which is the price of quality's genuine consent, and the reason this plan can go where the last one could not. The three functions are aligned not by exhortation but by removing the structural cause of the feud: today no one owns flow time, and each function's local metric provably damages the others (§11.1). We install a single accountable **Flow Owner**, one shared scorecard, an evidence rule (**no blame without a timestamp**), and a **Three-Way Treaty** in which each function surrenders one privilege and receives one guarantee. **Quoted lead time changes last, not first** (Gate 4): we earn the number, then we sell it.

---

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every day-count, percentage, inventory value and threshold below is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. The single most dangerous number in this company right now is a lead time we announce before we can hit it. That is precisely what happened last time.

### 0.2 What this covers

"Lead time" has been used internally to mean at least four different things, which is one reason the three functions cannot agree on where it goes.

| Term | Definition used in this document | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| **Quoted lead time** | What Sales writes on the proposal | Commercial, via §10 |
| **Promised date** | The confirmed date on order acknowledgement | Flow Owner, via capable-to-promise (§8.4) |
| **Actual order-to-delivery** | Clean-order date → goods available to ship | Flow Owner |
| **Touch time** | Hours in which material is transformed or verified | Production + Quality |
| **Flow efficiency** | Touch time ÷ actual order-to-delivery | Flow Owner |

**Rule of the document:** every claim about where time is lost is stated as a timestamped measurement or explicitly labelled a hypothesis. Assertions with neither status are not admissible in this programme (§11.4).

| Population | Illustrative share of order volume *[target — Gate 1 to measure]* | Nature | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lane 1 — Platform/standard** | ~[30]% | Catalogue configuration, no new engineering, pre-released BOM and pre-approved inspection plan | §5.2, target quote [4–6] wks |
| **Lane 2 — Configured** | ~[35]% | Options from an approved catalogue, parametric drawings, pre-approved ITP variants | §5.2, target quote [6–8] wks |
| **Lane 3 — Engineered** | ~[35]% | Genuine new engineering, novel certification path, customer-specific approvals | §5.2, quoted from slot calendar, honestly |
| **Aftermarket/spares** | — | Separate value stream, out of scope for v1.0, but *must not* be starved of capacity by this programme (§15) | Noted |

# WHERE AND HOW WE WORK
## A global operating framework for flexible work
**Executive Committee decision document | v2.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *structure* and the decision rights. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to write one work policy for the whole company.** A single global rule — "three days in office," "remote-first," "hybrid" — will be simultaneously too loose for the teams that need co-presence to function and too tight for the teams that don't, and it will be illegal, unaffordable or culturally illegible in a meaningful share of our countries. Instead, adopt a **federated model with three layers**: a thin, non-waivable **Global Spine** (eight commitments that make us one company); a **Country Dial** set by each market against a published dossier of legal, infrastructural and normative constraints; and a **Team Charter** — the real unit of decision — written by every team of roughly 6–15 people and reviewed twice a year. Work is designed against **five work modes and two overlays** (§4), not against days of the week. Offices are re-typed from desk inventory into a **four-format portfolio** whose feasibility depends on one piece of machinery we have never had: **cross-team anchor-day allocation** (§9.2). Roughly [X]% of our workforce cannot choose where they work at all; they are in scope from page one, not as an afterthought (§6). Fairness — proximity bias, geographic pay, apprenticeship — is engineered explicitly (§11), and output measurement is fixed *before* flexibility scales, because otherwise presence quietly becomes the proxy again (§12). **One constraint governs everything: the Subsidiarity Rule (§3) — each decision is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects, and no lower.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every ratio, day-count, square-metre figure, stipend value and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are included because a framework with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable framework cannot be improved. **Gate 1 (§16) replaces them with measured values**; the Committee approves the calibrated set before any policy is communicated to employees.

What we are asking the Committee to adopt today is: the three-layer structure, the eight Spine commitments, the five modes, the four office formats, the decision-rights matrix (Appendix C), the gate sequence, and the funding of Gate 1.

### 0.2 Who this covers

The phrase "future of work" has been used inside the company as a synonym for "hybrid office work." That framing excludes a large minority — possibly a majority — of our people, and it is the fastest route to a two-class company.

| Population | Illustrative share *[target — Gate 1 to measure]* | What flexibility means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Location-flexible** | ~[40]% | Where and when, within team and country limits | §§3–5, 7–12 |
| **B. Fixed-location** — manufacturing, warehouse, retail, lab, clinical, site security, catering, field maintenance | ~[45]% | **When**, not where: schedule predictability, shift choice, roster self-scheduling, compressed weeks, time-in-lieu, leave access | §6 (parallel framework, equal status) |
| **C. Mixed** — field service, sales, engineers with lab or site dependencies, plant supervisors | ~[15]% | Site-anchored days plus flexible remainder; the *anchor* is set by the site, the remainder by the Charter | §6.3 |

**Rule of the document:** wherever this framework grants something to population A, §6 states the equivalent grant to B and C, or explains why no equivalent exists. Wherever we report a fairness metric (§11.4), all three populations appear in the cut. A benefit that only knowledge workers can consume is not a benefit; it is a differential.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The debate has been framed as *remote vs. office*. That axis is unhelpful, because it treats location as the variable when location is a **consequence**.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How many days in the office? | What work do we do that is *degraded* by distance, and how much of it is there? |
| Is remote work productive? | Which roles have output that is legible without co-presence — and which have we simply never learned to measure? (§12) |
| How do we get people back? | What must the office be *good at* that a home desk isn't, and are our buildings currently good at it? |
| What's our policy? | Who decides, at what layer, with what evidence, and who hears the appeal? (§3, §15) |

**Corollary 1.** Attendance is not a goal. It is an input we may or may not need. A policy expressed *purely* as a day-count is a confession that the analysis wasn't done. (Day-count *bands* have exactly one legitimate use — real-estate planning and legal negotiation. That use is fenced in §7.3.)

**Corollary 2.** Most of the pain reported as "hybrid isn't working" is not about location. It is about **meeting load, unclear decision rights, documentation debt, time-zone tax and untrained managers**. Those are fixable independent of where anyone sits; they are cheaper than real estate; and they compound. **Sequence them first** (§16, Gate 2 wave 1).

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

**A gate, not a priority:** *Legal, tax and collective-agreement integrity.* No arrangement that creates permanent-establishment exposure, misclassifies employment, breaches a works-council agreement or violates working-time law. This is not ranked against anything; it is a pass/fail test applied before options are compared. Legal and Tax hold a veto, not an opinion.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Equity of opportunity** | A person's promotion odds are not predicted by their distance from a headquarters, their work pattern, or their population (A/B/C) |
| **2** | **Output quality and speed** | Team-level delivery against commitments, measured per §12 |
| **3** | **Cohesion** | Enough shared context that the company can change direction without fracturing |
| **4** | **Talent access** | Hiring and retention in labour markets a full-return policy would close to us |
| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

Equity outranks output because equity failures are slow, compounding and legally actionable, while output problems are visible and correctable. Cost is last because savings taken out of cohesion and equity are borrowed, not earned.

### 2.1 Adjudication — who breaks the tie

An unarbitrated priority list is decorative. Therefore:

- Conflicts between objectives are decided by the **Work Design Council** (§15.1) on a written submission that names the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost proposal that reduces equity or cohesion must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. "It's cheaper" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **CPO + CEO** sign-off and is entered in the Exception Register (§15.3) with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions internally. Precedent is how a federated model stays coherent without a rulebook.

---

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

Full decision rights, including who may *not* decide what, are in **Appendix C**.

### 3.1 The Global Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**S1 — Purpose before place.** Every requirement to be somewhere must name the work mode (§4) it serves. "Because it's Tuesday" is not a reason.

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S3 — Written-first for decisions, specs and context.** These live in a durable, searchable, permissioned place. *Scope limit:* S3 governs **decisions, specifications and context only**. It explicitly does **not** apply to 1:1s, coaching, sensitive feedback, performance conversations, wellbeing discussions or relationship time — documenting those would be both chilling and, in several jurisdictions, unlawful. The old formulation ("a meeting with no artefact did not happen") is withdrawn as absolutist; the replacement test is: *if a decision was made and is not written down, it will be re-made.*

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.
*Exception path (mandatory, because rotation is sometimes impossible):* where the counterparty is a customer, a market open, a regulator or a plant shift, a **Standing Unsociable-Hours Exception** may be granted by the regional leader for ≤12 months, renewable, entered in the Exception Register, and only with one of four compensating remedies named: (a) follow-the-sun redesign so the handoff replaces the meeting; (b) hiring or relocating for overlap; (c) time-in-lieu at a published rate; (d) an unsociable-hours allowance where local law and practice support it. An exception with no remedy is refused.

**S6 — Same job, same access.** Location and work pattern do not change eligibility for projects, promotion, sponsorship, budget or information. Where location changes *compensation*, the rule is published, zone-based and applied mechanically (§11.2).

**S7 — A baseline environment guarantee, for everyone.** Every employee has a safe, connected, ergonomically adequate place to work — at home, in a company office, at a paid third space, or **at their site**, at company cost, at levels set by the Country Dial. For population B this reads as facilities standards: rest space, lockers, connectivity, decent break areas, and equivalent per-head workplace spend. Population B must not fund population A's stipends out of its own neglected estate.

**S8 — Nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement.** No exceptions, no goodwill workarounds, no "just for this one hire."

Eight is the ceiling. Every additional global rule must be true simultaneously in Lagos, Stuttgart, Bengaluru, São Paulo, Osaka and Salt Lake City — and very few things are.

---

## §4 The five work modes and two overlays

Modes, not days, are the design unit. Sort a team's actual month into these five, apply the overlays, and its Charter largely writes itself.

### 4.1 The five modes (mutually exclusive; every hour lands in exactly one)

| # | Mode | Discriminating test | Distance sensitivity | Best setting | Primary enabler |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Deep focus** | One person producing; interruption is the enemy | **Negative** — co-presence usually *harms* it | **Any environment the individual controls and can reach reliably** — home study, quiet office zone, or a Touchdown site (§9.1) where home is not viable | Calendar protection; do-not-disturb norms |
| **M2** | **Convergent work** | *Someone has to change their mind or merge two positions.* Known problem, needs a decision | Low–moderate | Anywhere with good tooling; short sync after async pre-read | Pre-read + 30-min call + written decision |
| **M3** | **Divergent work** | *Nobody knows the answer yet.* Ambiguity, generation, productive conflict, whiteboarding | **High** | Same room, writable walls, 2–6 hour blocks | In-person workshop; digital canvas as an honest second-best |
| **M4** | **Apprenticeship and tacit transfer** | *Someone is learning judgement that isn't written down.* | **Very high** | Same room, sustained, with unscheduled overhearing | Co-location blocks; work-alongs; senior time budget (§11.3) |
| **M5** | **Coordination and handoff** | *Someone needs to know something at the right time.* Status, dependencies, handoffs | Low, **if disciplined** | Nowhere in particular | Written status; overlap window; single source of truth |

M2 vs M5 is the distinction teams get wrong. **Changing a mind is M2. Transferring knowledge is M5.** If a recurring meeting only transmits information, it is M5 and should be a document.

### 4.2 The two overlays (not modes — do not allocate percentages to them)

- **Overlay T — Trust formation.** Relational credit is an *investment* that makes M2 and M3 cheap, not a mode of work. It is therefore handled as a **named budget and cadence** — offsites, shared meals, travel — owned at the Charter level and funded per §14.3. Design target *[target]*: every distributed team is physically together **at least twice a year**, and no employee goes **more than six months** without being in a room with colleagues. Treating trust as a byproduct is how distributed teams die quietly.
- **Overlay C — Customer, site and shift override.** For customer-facing, field and site-dependent work, location is determined by the customer or the asset, not by us. This eliminates the double-counting that a "customer-facing mode" would have guaranteed.

| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.

# Critique: "Lead Time as a Design Problem" (v1.0 draft)

## 1. The fatal issue: the deliverable does not exist yet

The output stops mid-sentence in §1, Corollary 1. Everything the request actually asked for is referenced but not written:

- **Where time is lost** → deferred to §4.3 "order forensics" (not written)
- **Process/inventory/scheduling/supplier changes** → §5, §8 (not written); *no supplier change of any kind is named anywhere*, not even in the summary
- **How to protect quality gates** → §7.4 trip-wire, one sentence
- **How to align the three functions** → §11, one sentence each on Flow Owner / treaty / evidence rule
- Appendix A (decision rights) → referenced, absent

What exists is a frame, a governing rule, a definitions table, a lane taxonomy, and a rhetorical stance. That is perhaps 15% of the ask. Any assessment below is of scaffolding, not of a plan.

## 2. Structural inheritance from the previous document is doing damage

The draft has cloned the flexible-work doc's genre wholesale: "Executive Committee decision document," "The answer in one paragraph," "§0.1 Status of the numbers," "Stating the problem correctly" wrong/right table, "Corollary 1," "Rule of the document," Gate 1–4, calibration deferral, a single named governing rule as an analogue to the Subsidiarity Rule.

Some of this transfers well (see §7 below). Two elements transfer badly:

- **Calibration deferral is much weaker justification here.** A global work policy genuinely lacks baseline data. A manufacturer with certified inspections, routers, POs and NCRs has ERP/MES timestamps, and a competent value-stream walk of ten orders yields the answer in three weeks. Writing "[10–20]% flow efficiency *[target]*" and pushing all substance to Gate 1 reads as a stalling device, not as intellectual honesty. The draft should instead specify the **exact data extraction list** (operation start/stop from router confirmations, PO placed/promised/received, inspection-requested vs inspection-performed timestamps, NCR open/disposition/close, engineering release vs first PO release, dossier assembly start/ship) and state what to do where timestamps *don't* exist (manual tagging of 20–30 live orders; physical walk of 5).
- **Gate purism is commercially expensive.** "Quoted lead time changes last, not first (Gate 4)" is defensible discipline, but the company is losing one deal in three *now*. The plan needs an interim commercial bridge — a small capacity-reserved fast lane for selected customers, conditional/date-banded quotes, published on-time reliability as a differentiator — rather than asking Sales to lose deals for four gates.

## 3. The Non-Transformation Rule is the best idea in the draft and is mis-stated

As written — "time may be removed only where no material is being transformed and no verification is being performed" — the rule contradicts three of the five lever classes the same paragraph endorses:

- **Prevention / first-time-yield** changes transformation.
- **Verification latency reduction** operates on verification.
- Legitimate engineering (setup reduction, tooling, fixturing, cycle-time work) removes touch time and is forbidden by the literal rule, though it is exactly what a mature operation should do.

Worse, the absolutist companion claim — "one prohibited class: reducing what we inspect" — forfeits a likely major saving. After a warranty spike, organisations reliably bolt on **defensive, non-certified inspection** (duplicate dimensional checks, 100% re-inspection of previously sampled features, extra sign-offs). That is not certified quality; it is scar tissue. The rule should distinguish:

1. **Certified / regulatory / customer-witnessed inspection content** — untouchable in scope, sampling and acceptance criteria; only its *logistics* (when, where, by whom, with what gauge, in what parallel sequence) is in play, and any ITP change goes through change control and, where applicable, the notified body or customer approval.
2. **Internally added inspection** — reviewable, but only via documented risk assessment with a Quality veto and a recorded rationale.

Without that split, the rule is both unfollowable and self-defeating.

## 4. Internal numerical inconsistency

- Title promises **[6–7] weeks**. Lane table gives Lane 1 [4–6], Lane 2 [6–8], Lane 3 slot-based. A 6–7 week headline is not derivable from those lanes, and 35% of volume is explicitly excluded from any week number.
- The summary claims "**[60–70]% of demand … can be quoted at [6] weeks**." The lane table says Lane 1 + Lane 2 = 65%, but Lane 2 is quoted at **6–8**. The headline and the table disagree.
- The summary asserts "[10–20]% flow efficiency is typical in chains of this type" as a benchmark while tagging it *[target]* — conflating industry benchmark with internal design target. It also violates the draft's own §0.2 rule ("every claim about where time is lost is stated as a timestamped measurement or explicitly labelled a hypothesis") in the very first paragraph.
- 14 weeks is silently converted to "70 working days" in §1. Quoted lead time to a customer is calendar time and includes supplier calendar days, holidays and shutdowns. Make the conversion explicit or the flow-efficiency arithmetic is wrong.
- **Benchmark parity is never established.** The 14-vs-6 comparison may be partly apples-to-oranges: the competitor may quote standard product only, ship from finished stock, quote ex-works vs our DDP, or exclude customer drawing-approval time. A competitive offer teardown (scope, terms, incoterms, configurability, penalty regime) is a cheap, high-value Gate 1 task and is missing.

## 5. Missing content that should appear even in a skeleton

- **Suppliers.** Purchased long-lead items (castings, gearboxes, large bearings, motors, hydraulic assemblies, control cabinets, pressure parts) commonly dominate a 14-week quote and cannot be fixed by internal queue removal. Nothing on: capacity reservation agreements, blanket POs with pull release, consignment/VMI, dual sourcing, supplier lead-time buy-down, kit-completeness measurement, **or delegated source inspection / PPAP to eliminate incoming inspection queues**.
- **Inventory cost of the promise.** A decoupling point is named but never priced. Six weeks is bought with semi-finished platform stock and long-lead safety stock; that is working capital, obsolescence risk and a Finance sign-off. The draft asks "what did the competitor give up?" and then declines to answer even hypothetically.
- **Scheduling mechanics.** No load levelling, no constraint identification, no CONWIP/pull, no finite-capacity scheduling, no order-release freeze window, no engineering-change cut-off, and crucially **no treatment of certified inspectors and witness slots as a scheduled, capacity-planned resource** (inspector qualification pipelines run months — that is a hard capacity constraint, not an attitude problem).
- **Quality-gate acceleration specifics.** Missing: in-line/at-station inspection, SPC on the features the ITP checks, gauge and fixture provisioning, inspector cross-training, NCR/MRB disposition SLA, first-article strategy, **continuous dossier assembly instead of end-of-line documentation build** (often 1–2 weeks of pure paperwork queue), digital records/e-signature, third-party and customer witness scheduling protocol.
- **Engineering is absent.** The framing is "three feuding functions," but engineering release, drawing approval loops and change orders are usually the largest single block of elapsed time in configured/engineered equipment. Either bring Engineering in as a fourth party to the Treaty or justify its exclusion.
- **Root cause of the last failure.** The draft asserts the previous compression removed the wrong class of time. Plausible, but unevidenced — the warranty spike more likely came from overtime, out-of-sequence build, unqualified substitutes, concurrent ECOs, or new suppliers. Without a retrospective on the actual failure mechanism, the trip-wire may guard the wrong door and the plan loses its credibility claim.
- **Business case.** Value of the one-in-three lost deals, programme cost, inventory bill, payback. An Exco document without this cannot be approved.
- **Demand response.** Quoting 6 weeks will shift mix and volume upward; capacity and win-rate consequences are unmodelled.

## 6. Design flaws in what *is* specified

- **Trip-wire brittleness.** "Freeze all lead-time reduction if FTY, escapes or audit findings move the wrong way" will trip on noise. Needs control limits / statistical decision rules, graduated response (pause a lane vs freeze programme), a named un-freeze authority, and — because warranty claims lag by months — **cohort tracking of units built under the new flow** as the true verification, not just leading indicators.
- **Lane classification will be gamed.** Sales has every incentive to book Lane 3 work at Lane 1 dates. Needs an independent classifier, a rule that Lane 3 cannot be quoted from the Lane 1 calendar, and a priced "special request" path.
- **Flow Owner authority undefined.** A single accountable owner across Production, Quality and Sales only works with stated authority over order release, sequencing and promise-dating, and stated *non*-authority over inspection content. Say so.
- **"Clean order" is load-bearing but undefined**, and it is the mechanism by which Sales-side delay gets excluded from the metric. Define it, and measure the *pre*-clean-order interval separately or Sales will pass its queue into the invisible column.

## 7. What is genuinely good and should survive rewrite

- The four-way disambiguation of "lead time" (quoted / promised / actual / touch time) plus flow efficiency — this alone dissolves much of the inter-functional argument.
- Lane segmentation against a deliberate decoupling point instead of one padded average.
- The trip-wire as the *price of quality's consent* — the right political instrument.
- "No blame without a timestamp" and the Treaty's give-one/get-one symmetry.
- Corollary 1 (quote = median + variance buffer) is the single most useful analytical sentence in the draft; it implies that improving DIFOT shortens the quote without touching the build, and should be promoted to a headline lever.

## 8. Presentation

The one-paragraph summary is ~450 words in a single block with heavy bolding — unreadable at the density it attempts. The aphorism rate ("we are not slow at building; we are slow at waiting") is high enough to read as performance rather than analysis, and self-praise ("the reason this plan can go where the last one could not") is unearned in a document with no evidence yet.

---

**Priority fixes:** (1) finish the document — §§3–15 and Appendix A; (2) restate the Non-Transformation Rule with the certified-vs-internally-added split; (3) reconcile the 6–7 week headline with the lane table; (4) add supplier, inventory-cost, scheduling and dossier content; (5) bring Engineering into the alignment mechanism; (6) add the business case and an interim commercial bridge; (7) replace generic "Gate 1 will measure" with a named 4-week diagnostic, data list, owner and 3 no-regret actions starting immediately.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**

So the plan is governed by one rule: **time may be removed only where no material is being transformed and no verification is being performed** (§3, the *Non-Transformation Rule*). Within that rule there are five legitimate lever classes — queue removal, capacity addition, prevention (first-time yield), scope segmentation, and verification *latency* reduction with verification *content* untouched — and one prohibited class: reducing what we inspect. We then stop selling one lead time to everyone: orders are sorted into **three fulfilment lanes** against a deliberately placed customisation decoupling point (§5), so that the [60–70]%*[target]* of demand that is genuinely configurable-from-platform can be quoted at [6] weeks while genuinely engineered orders are quoted honestly from a capacity-slot calendar instead of being hidden inside a padded average. Quality gates are not weakened; they are **accelerated and made non-negotiable in the same instrument**, protected by an automatic trip-wire that freezes all lead-time reduction if first-time yield, escaping defects or audit findings move the wrong way (§7.4) — which is the price of quality's genuine consent, and the reason this plan can go where the last one could not. The three functions are aligned not by exhortation but by removing the structural cause of the feud: today no one owns flow time, and each function's local metric provably damages the others (§11.1). We install a single accountable **Flow Owner**, one shared scorecard, an evidence rule (**no blame without a timestamp**), and a **Three-Way Treaty** in which each function surrenders one privilege and receives one guarantee. **Quoted lead time changes last, not first** (Gate 4): we earn the number, then we sell it.

# Critique: "Lead Time as a Design Problem" (v1.0 draft)

## 1. The fatal issue: the deliverable does not exist yet

The output stops mid-sentence in §1, Corollary 1. Everything the request actually asked for is referenced but not written:

- **Where time is lost** → deferred to §4.3 "order forensics" (not written)
- **Process/inventory/scheduling/supplier changes** → §5, §8 (not written); *no supplier change of any kind is named anywhere*, not even in the summary
- **How to protect quality gates** → §7.4 trip-wire, one sentence
- **How to align the three functions** → §11, one sentence each on Flow Owner / treaty / evidence rule
- Appendix A (decision rights) → referenced, absent

What exists is a frame, a governing rule, a definitions table, a lane taxonomy, and a rhetorical stance. That is perhaps 15% of the ask. Any assessment below is of scaffolding, not of a plan.

## 2. Structural inheritance from the previous document is doing damage

The draft has cloned the flexible-work doc's genre wholesale: "Executive Committee decision document," "The answer in one paragraph," "§0.1 Status of the numbers," "Stating the problem correctly" wrong/right table, "Corollary 1," "Rule of the document," Gate 1–4, calibration deferral, a single named governing rule as an analogue to the Subsidiarity Rule.

Some of this transfers well (see §7 below). Two elements transfer badly:

- **Calibration deferral is much weaker justification here.** A global work policy genuinely lacks baseline data. A manufacturer with certified inspections, routers, POs and NCRs has ERP/MES timestamps, and a competent value-stream walk of ten orders yields the answer in three weeks. Writing "[10–20]% flow efficiency *[target]*" and pushing all substance to Gate 1 reads as a stalling device, not as intellectual honesty. The draft should instead specify the **exact data extraction list** (operation start/stop from router confirmations, PO placed/promised/received, inspection-requested vs inspection-performed timestamps, NCR open/disposition/close, engineering release vs first PO release, dossier assembly start/ship) and state what to do where timestamps *don't* exist (manual tagging of 20–30 live orders; physical walk of 5).
- **Gate purism is commercially expensive.** "Quoted lead time changes last, not first (Gate 4)" is defensible discipline, but the company is losing one deal in three *now*. The plan needs an interim commercial bridge — a small capacity-reserved fast lane for selected customers, conditional/date-banded quotes, published on-time reliability as a differentiator — rather than asking Sales to lose deals for four gates.

## 3. The Non-Transformation Rule is the best idea in the draft and is mis-stated

As written — "time may be removed only where no material is being transformed and no verification is being performed" — the rule contradicts three of the five lever classes the same paragraph endorses:

- **Prevention / first-time-yield** changes transformation.
- **Verification latency reduction** operates on verification.
- Legitimate engineering (setup reduction, tooling, fixturing, cycle-time work) removes touch time and is forbidden by the literal rule, though it is exactly what a mature operation should do.

Worse, the absolutist companion claim — "one prohibited class: reducing what we inspect" — forfeits a likely major saving. After a warranty spike, organisations reliably bolt on **defensive, non-certified inspection** (duplicate dimensional checks, 100% re-inspection of previously sampled features, extra sign-offs). That is not certified quality; it is scar tissue. The rule should distinguish:

1. **Certified / regulatory / customer-witnessed inspection content** — untouchable in scope, sampling and acceptance criteria; only its *logistics* (when, where, by whom, with what gauge, in what parallel sequence) is in play, and any ITP change goes through change control and, where applicable, the notified body or customer approval.
2. **Internally added inspection** — reviewable, but only via documented risk assessment with a Quality veto and a recorded rationale.

Without that split, the rule is both unfollowable and self-defeating.

## 4. Internal numerical inconsistency

- Title promises **[6–7] weeks**. Lane table gives Lane 1 [4–6], Lane 2 [6–8], Lane 3 slot-based. A 6–7 week headline is not derivable from those lanes, and 35% of volume is explicitly excluded from any week number.
- The summary claims "**[60–70]% of demand … can be quoted at [6] weeks**." The lane table says Lane 1 + Lane 2 = 65%, but Lane 2 is quoted at **6–8**. The headline and the table disagree.
- The summary asserts "[10–20]% flow efficiency is typical in chains of this type" as a benchmark while tagging it *[target]* — conflating industry benchmark with internal design target. It also violates the draft's own §0.2 rule ("every claim about where time is lost is stated as a timestamped measurement or explicitly labelled a hypothesis") in the very first paragraph.
- 14 weeks is silently converted to "70 working days" in §1. Quoted lead time to a customer is calendar time and includes supplier calendar days, holidays and shutdowns. Make the conversion explicit or the flow-efficiency arithmetic is wrong.
- **Benchmark parity is never established.** The 14-vs-6 comparison may be partly apples-to-oranges: the competitor may quote standard product only, ship from finished stock, quote ex-works vs our DDP, or exclude customer drawing-approval time. A competitive offer teardown (scope, terms, incoterms, configurability, penalty regime) is a cheap, high-value Gate 1 task and is missing.

## 5. Missing content that should appear even in a skeleton

- **Suppliers.** Purchased long-lead items (castings, gearboxes, large bearings, motors, hydraulic assemblies, control cabinets, pressure parts) commonly dominate a 14-week quote and cannot be fixed by internal queue removal. Nothing on: capacity reservation agreements, blanket POs with pull release, consignment/VMI, dual sourcing, supplier lead-time buy-down, kit-completeness measurement, **or delegated source inspection / PPAP to eliminate incoming inspection queues**.
- **Inventory cost of the promise.** A decoupling point is named but never priced. Six weeks is bought with semi-finished platform stock and long-lead safety stock; that is working capital, obsolescence risk and a Finance sign-off. The draft asks "what did the competitor give up?" and then declines to answer even hypothetically.
- **Scheduling mechanics.** No load levelling, no constraint identification, no CONWIP/pull, no finite-capacity scheduling, no order-release freeze window, no engineering-change cut-off, and crucially **no treatment of certified inspectors and witness slots as a scheduled, capacity-planned resource** (inspector qualification pipelines run months — that is a hard capacity constraint, not an attitude problem).
- **Quality-gate acceleration specifics.** Missing: in-line/at-station inspection, SPC on the features the ITP checks, gauge and fixture provisioning, inspector cross-training, NCR/MRB disposition SLA, first-article strategy, **continuous dossier assembly instead of end-of-line documentation build** (often 1–2 weeks of pure paperwork queue), digital records/e-signature, third-party and customer witness scheduling protocol.
- **Engineering is absent.** The framing is "three feuding functions," but engineering release, drawing approval loops and change orders are usually the largest single block of elapsed time in configured/engineered equipment. Either bring Engineering in as a fourth party to the Treaty or justify its exclusion.
- **Root cause of the last failure.** The draft asserts the previous compression removed the wrong class of time. Plausible, but unevidenced — the warranty spike more likely came from overtime, out-of-sequence build, unqualified substitutes, concurrent ECOs, or new suppliers. Without a retrospective on the actual failure mechanism, the trip-wire may guard the wrong door and the plan loses its credibility claim.
- **Business case.** Value of the one-in-three lost deals, programme cost, inventory bill, payback. An Exco document without this cannot be approved.
- **Demand response.** Quoting 6 weeks will shift mix and volume upward; capacity and win-rate consequences are unmodelled.

## 6. Design flaws in what *is* specified

- **Trip-wire brittleness.** "Freeze all lead-time reduction if FTY, escapes or audit findings move the wrong way" will trip on noise. Needs control limits / statistical decision rules, graduated response (pause a lane vs freeze programme), a named un-freeze authority, and — because warranty claims lag by months — **cohort tracking of units built under the new flow** as the true verification, not just leading indicators.
- **Lane classification will be gamed.** Sales has every incentive to book Lane 3 work at Lane 1 dates. Needs an independent classifier, a rule that Lane 3 cannot be quoted from the Lane 1 calendar, and a priced "special request" path.
- **Flow Owner authority undefined.** A single accountable owner across Production, Quality and Sales only works with stated authority over order release, sequencing and promise-dating, and stated *non*-authority over inspection content. Say so.
- **"Clean order" is load-bearing but undefined**, and it is the mechanism by which Sales-side delay gets excluded from the metric. Define it, and measure the *pre*-clean-order interval separately or Sales will pass its queue into the invisible column.

## 7. What is genuinely good and should survive rewrite

- The four-way disambiguation of "lead time" (quoted / promised / actual / touch time) plus flow efficiency — this alone dissolves much of the inter-functional argument.
- Lane segmentation against a deliberate decoupling point instead of one padded average.
- The trip-wire as the *price of quality's consent* — the right political instrument.
- "No blame without a timestamp" and the Treaty's give-one/get-one symmetry.
- Corollary 1 (quote = median + variance buffer) is the single most useful analytical sentence in the draft; it implies that improving DIFOT shortens the quote without touching the build, and should be promoted to a headline lever.

## 8. Presentation

The one-paragraph summary is ~450 words in a single block with heavy bolding — unreadable at the density it attempts. The aphorism rate ("we are not slow at building; we are slow at waiting") is high enough to read as performance rather than analysis, and self-praise ("the reason this plan can go where the last one could not") is unearned in a document with no evidence yet.

## Summary

**The commercial situation.** We quote 14 weeks; our fastest competitor quotes 6; Sales reports losing one deal in three on delivery speed. We also carry the memory of a compression attempt that produced a warranty spike and two years of reputational repair. Both facts are now constraints on any plan: it must move the quoted number materially, and it must be structurally incapable of repeating the earlier failure.

**Where the time is.** Our working hypothesis — stated so it can be falsified in four weeks, not asserted — is that of the 98 calendar days we quote, roughly 20 days are engineering-release and drawing-approval elapsed time, 30 days are long-lead purchased material, and about 25 days are queue: waiting for an inspector, a witness slot, an NCR disposition, a kit to complete, or a document pack to be assembled at the end of the line. Actual transformation and verification is on the order of 100–110 hours. The build is not the problem.

**What we will and will not touch.** Certified inspection *content* — scope, sampling plan, acceptance criteria, hold points — is untouchable. Its *logistics* — when it happens, where, by whom, with which gauge, in parallel with what — is entirely in play, and is where the largest single tranche of recoverable time sits. Separately, the inspection layer we added *ourselves* after the last warranty spike (duplicate checks, 100% re-inspection of sampled features, extra sign-offs) is not certified quality; it is reviewable, but only through documented risk assessment with a Quality veto (§3).

**The five things that actually change.**
1. **Segmentation.** Stop selling one padded average. Three lanes against a deliberately placed decoupling point: platform (4 weeks), configured (7 weeks), engineered (slot-dated, honestly 12–16 weeks). Weighted quoted average falls from 14 to ~8.2 weeks, and ~70% of volume becomes competitive with the 6-week rival.
2. **Suppliers.** Long-lead purchased content is the single biggest block and cannot be fixed internally: capacity reservation agreements, blanket POs with pull release, consignment on the top-20 long-lead items, dual sourcing on the three sole-source constraints, and delegated source inspection to eliminate the incoming-inspection queue.
3. **Quality-gate acceleration.** Inspectors and witness slots become a capacity-planned, scheduled resource (their qualification pipeline runs months — this is a hard constraint, not an attitude); inspection moves to the station; the certification dossier is assembled continuously instead of built at the end.
4. **Variance, not just speed.** A quote is the median actual plus a buffer sized by our own unreliability. If delivery-in-full-on-time is around 65%, several weeks of our 14 are pure protection. Raising DIFOT shortens the quote without touching the build — the cheapest lever we have.
5. **Ownership.** No one currently owns flow time, and each function's local metric measurably damages the others'. We install one accountable Flow Owner with defined authority over release, sequencing and promise-dating — and explicitly *no* authority over inspection content — plus a shared scorecard, an evidence rule ("no blame without a timestamp"), and a treaty in which each of four functions (Engineering included) surrenders one privilege and receives one guarantee.

**Quality protection.** A graduated trip-wire with statistical decision rules, and — because warranty claims lag by months — cohort tracking of every unit built under the new flow for 12 months. Quality holds the un-freeze authority jointly with the CEO. This is the price of Quality's genuine consent to the programme.

**Commercial bridge.** Sales cannot be asked to lose deals for six months. From week 4 we run a capacity-reserved fast lane (limited slots, priced), date-banded conditional quotes, and published on-time reliability as a differentiator.

**Money.** Illustratively: ~$13M/yr incremental contribution from recovered win rate, plus ~$1.8M/yr of expediting and premium-freight avoidance, against $3.2M programme opex, $4.5M capex and ~$7M net additional working capital. Payback under two years, with sensitivity in §13.3.
